title: Council backs Ontario Energy Board gas subsidy decision
subtitle: Also: 2024 property tax ratios, private tree by-law, internal audit plan, and parkland fee waiver for shelter.
overview: Council voted to support the Ontario Energy Board's decision to end the subsidy for gas pipelines serving new developments, and asked the province to withdraw Bill 165 {{vote:m6}}. The motion will be sent to the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, the Premier, two provincial ministers, the local MPP and all Ontario municipalities. It is a statement of position and does not change city services.

Supporters pointed to climate targets, long-term costs for gas customers and provincial involvement in an independent regulator. The Mayor said the issue was complicated, noted that the decision is under appeal, and did not support the motion.

Council also approved a consent package covering the 2024 property tax ratios and rates, the private tree protection by-law update and the 2024–2026 internal audit work plan. Council waived parkland dedication fees for the emergency shelter renovation and expansion planned for 23 Gordon Street {{vote:m5}}, which lowers a cost for that project.

decisions.item: Support for Ontario Energy Board gas decision
decisions.detail: Council expressed support for ending the fossil gas infrastructure subsidy, asked the province to withdraw Bill 165, and will circulate the resolution to provincial leaders and municipalities {{vote:m6}}.
Council waived any applicable parkland dedication fees for the emergency shelter renovation and expansion planned for 23 Gordon Street {{vote:m5}}.
Council approved the 2024 property tax ratios and corresponding tax rates set out in the staff report.
Council received the key issues and options report and directed staff to proceed with its recommendations.
Council approved the internal audit work plan and the Value-for-Money Audit Review Framework, and received the Internal Audit Charter update.

debate: Delegates argued the subsidy lets gas utility costs for new connections fall on existing gas customers, unlike hydro, water and wastewater connections, which developers pay for.

Several delegates, including students, said new gas lines last about 60 years and conflict with net zero 2050 goals. They said heat pumps can be cheaper to run and that the decision supports both housing affordability and climate goals.
Delegates said the Energy Board decision followed a year-long hearing and is not a gas ban. One said the board warned of stranded assets if gas demand falls.
One councillor asked about backup heat during power outages. The mover said heat pumps do not require a backup and battery backups are an option. Staff had no information on hand.

Councillors in favour said provincial interference in an independent regulator is comparable to ministerial zoning orders. The Mayor opposed the motion, saying the issue was complex and the decision is under appeal.
